Incluso hoy, la familia se reúne para comer ese platillo.</p><p>El platillo les recuerda cuando su papá lo cocinaba para ellos de niños.</p><p>“A mi papá le encanta analizar los platillos y ver cómo puedes mejorarlos, así que eso era parte de la diversión”, recordó Alexis Vejar. “Es algo que Teddy y yo comíamos mucho en Morelia porque había un puestito que vendía cochinita pibil. Íbamos directos al lugar pequeñito que vendía esos tacos chiquitos con las cebollitas rojas encima. Estábamos obsesionados con ellos. Nos recordaba muchísimo a casa”.</p><p>Al recordar su tiempo en México, Alexis y Teddy reflexionaron sobre lo simples que parecían las recetas en teoría, aunque ahora se dan cuenta del inmenso tiempo y proceso que todo ello implicaba. Se cultivaba y cosechaba el maíz, luego pasaba por el proceso de nixtamalización, una tradición que mantienen hoy en su restaurante para elaborar sus propias tortillas caseras.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OazrsIWZC3Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Tastes from Home: Tortillas, togetherness and time well spent."></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“Cada vez que visitábamos a mi abuela, ella se despertaba y hacía pan casero con levadura natural que ella misma cultivaba en un horno de leña”, recordó Alexis Vejar. “Si teníamos crema o queso, ella ordeñaba la vaca para hacerlo. Si había carne, era carne que ellos criaban, que faenaban, que curaban. Los menús estaban limitados por lo que había disponible en la granja”.</p><p>Aunque llevan años en el negocio, Alexis y Teddy dicen que todavía están aprendiendo y creciendo.</p><div entries.title: ¿Están demoliendo el Hawthorne Race Course para construir un centro de datos? Cicero cree que sí
entries.summary: <p>Las autoridades de Cicero creen que podría haber planes para un centro de datos que reemplace al Hawthorne Race Course, que cerró recientemente tras 135 años de carreras de caballos.</p><p>Como símbolo de lo impopulares que se han vuelto los desarrollos de centros de datos, se esperaba que los fideicomisarios del suburbio del oeste consideraran dos resoluciones que se oponen a los centros de datos cuando se reunieran este martes, aunque no se han hecho anuncios oficiales sobre ningún proyecto.</p><p>En todo Illinois, residentes y municipios locales están rechazando los grandes centros de datos que se desarrollan para apoyar la inteligencia artificial (AI). Esos centros consumen mucha energía, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/14/clientes-de-comed-podran-enfrentar-un-aumento-de-dos-digitos-en-sus-facturas-de-luz" target="_blank" >incrementan las facturas eléctricas residenciales</a>, consumen enormes cantidades de agua y generan ruido y otras molestias.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ea0000" name="module-ea0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Una de las resoluciones que se presentarán ante los fideicomisarios se opone a un centro de datos en la propiedad de Hawthorne cercana, aunque no ha habido reconocimiento público de que exista tal plan. La resolución dice que las autoridades de la localidad no quieren que se construyan proyectos en ningún lugar cerca del poblado de Cicero, hogar de más de 80,000 personas.</p><p>Un comprador misterioso con el nombre de Allimac 2023 LLC acordó pagar $90 millones por la propiedad localizada en 3501 S Laramie Ave. en Stickney, suburbio que colinda con Cicero. El propietario no se ha identificado públicamente ni ha dicho qué hará con el terreno.</p><p>“El desarrollo de un centro de datos en la propiedad de Hawthorne adyacente a [Cicero] impondrá una carga indebida sobre los recursos e infraestructura de la localidad”, establece la resolución propuesta, que también señala una posible amenaza para la salud pública.</p><p>La otra resolución que las autoridades de Cicero están considerando resulta un tanto desconcertante porque sugiere que otro organismo gubernamental está en conversaciones con un promotor inmobiliario para construir un centro de datos separado junto a la Planta de Reclamación de Agua de Stickney, que procesa cientos de millones de galones de agua al día, lo que la convierte en una de las mayores plantas de tratamiento de aguas residuales del mundo.</p><p>Un sitio web de la industria de centros de datos afirmó que existe un acuerdo en marcha para construir un centro de datos cerca de la planta de Stickney en los próximos dos años.</p><p>Sin embargo, la agencia gubernamental que opera la planta de aguas residuales, el Distrito Metropolitano de Reclamación de Agua del Gran Chicago (MWRD), niega que exista tal acuerdo.</p><p>“El distrito no tiene absolutamente ningún plan para un centro de datos y nunca emprendería ninguna iniciativa que afecte a nuestros vecinos sin antes consultar a la comunidad local para asegurar que se escuchen sus voces”, dijo la agencia en un comunicado. “Tenemos una excelente relación con el poblado de Cicero y nunca querríamos poner en riesgo esa relación”.</p><p>El 24 de julio, el distrito envió un correo electrónico a una empresa llamada MicroLink y le exigió que retirara una afirmación en un sitio web de la industria que indicaba que planeaba construir un centro de datos cerca de la planta de tratamiento de aguas residuales de Stickney con una fecha de proyecto en 2028, añadió el comunicado.</p><p>Ni MicroLink ni el sitio web de la industria de Baxtel respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios.</p><p>Sin citar fuentes, las autoridades de Cicero dijeron en un comunicado al Chicago Sun-Times que “las autoridades municipales se enteraron de un acuerdo que, según afirma un promotor inmobiliario, ya alcanzó con el MWRD para construir un centro de datos en una propiedad que limita con Cicero. Esperamos que el director de la agencia y su personal puedan explicar cómo un promotor inmobiliario puede ofrecer detalles tan específicos de un acuerdo sin que el público los conozca”.</p><p>En cuanto al rumoreado proyecto en el Hawthorne Race Course, “la municipalidad no quiso esperar a que comenzara la construcción antes de tomar medidas para proteger a los residentes de Cicero que literalmente viven al cruzar la calle”.</p><p>Josh Brniak, administrador de construcción y zonificación de Stickney, dijo que no sabe qué querrá hacer el nuevo propietario con el sitio. No ha habido contacto con Allimac, aseguró.</p><p>“Estábamos esperando a que se aprobara la venta”, comentó Brniak. “Ahora esperamos los próximos pasos”.</p><p>Las últimas carreras en Hawthorne, que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/03/05/hawthorne-race-course-icono-de-134-anos-en-las-carreras-de-caballos-de-chicago-se-declara-en-bancarrota" target="_blank" >solicitó protección bancaria bajo el Capítulo 11</a> en febrero, fueron el 19 de julio.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago dries out, cleans up, assessed damage after Monday's severe storms
entries.summary: <p><b></b> </p><p>People across the greater Chicago area on Tuesday were dealing with the effects of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" >heavy thunderstorms and damaging winds</a> from the day before. </p><p>A clear, sunny day brought some relief, as floodwaters receded, basements started to dry out, damages were assessed and power was being restored across the region.</p><p>In Downers Grove, meanwhile, a contractor who was working in a sewer when the storm hit remains missing, <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/contractor-remains-missing-being-trapped-downers-grove-sewer-curtiss-street-1-rescued/19589736/ " target="_blank" >according to ABC7</a>. Another worker who was in the sewer at the time has been found safe. Tuesday morning, police blocked off an area from Gilbert Avenue to Curtiss Street, with multiple firetrucks and ambulances in the area, ABC7 reported. <b></b> </p><p></p><p><b></b></p><p></p><p><b></b> Big wind gusts were recorded across the city and suburbs, topping out at 82 mph recorded in Waukegan, according to the National Weather Service. Midway Airport recorded winds of 73 mph, and O'Hare Airport saw 65 mph winds. In northwest Indiana, Valparaiso saw 64 mph gusts.</p><p> With the high winds came heavy rain, overwhelming streets and drainage systems. Chicago's official climate station at O'Hare measured 1.76 inches of rain, while Midway received 2.94 inches. Much of the Chicago area saw two to four inches of rain.</p><p>In some pockets of Cook County those two inches of rain falling in just two hours, according to the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District. </p><p>The two major reservoirs managing that rainfall both are filling, according to the MWRD, with McCook Reservoir about 56% full, storing nearly 2 billion gallons. The Thornton Reservoir, to the south, is about 34% full, storing nearly 2.7 billion gallons.</p><p>The weather service sent out storm survey teams Tuesday to determine whether tornadoes touched down in southern Cook County, focusing on Harvey and Lansing, and in DuPage County, including Carol Stream and Glen Ellyn.</p><p>The city's Office of Emergency Management and Communications reported 2,322 tree emergency calls and 973 reports of tree debris. There have also been 623 reports of water on streets, 599 flooded basements and 47 flooded viaducts around Chicago as well as 310 traffic signals out, 220 streetlights out, 160 downed wires and 116 damaged streetlight poles as of Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>According to ComEd, more than 530,000 electric customers lost power. By Tuesday morning, utility crews had restored electricity to nearly 300,000 customers, according to ComEd, which expects that by noon Wednesday, it will have restoredpower to about 80% of those who lost their electricity. The rest of ComEd customers will have power restored by 10 p.m. Friday, according to the utility.</p><p>Officials said the communities hit hardest during from Monday’s storm include Chicago Heights, Maywood, Crestwood, Bolingbrook, University Park, Libertyville and portions of the South Side.</p><p>The Illinois American Red Cross has also opened two shelters, in Steger and Gurnee, to help those impacted by the storm. According to regional communications director Connie Esparza, many Illinoisans have come to the shelter for access to electricity and food, with some staying overnight.</p><p>As cleanup efforts continue, officials are urging residents to avoid downed power lines, report hazards and use caution while traveling through areas still affected by flooding, fallen trees and power outages.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson explains why he hasn't decided whether to seek a second term
entries.summary: <p>A day before driving his oldest son to college, an emotional Brandon Johnson said Tuesday he would like to “hold on to this moment for a little while longer” — both as father and as Chicago’s mayor — before deciding whether to seek a second term.</p><p>Johnson said he allowed unnamed supporters to start circulating his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/28/chicagos-mayoral-campaign-circulation-nominating-petitions-johnson-giannoulias-quigley-mendoza-pappas-brewer" >nominating petitions Tuesday</a>, the first day to start gathering the 12,500 signatures needed to get on the ballot. He said he was encouraged by the "number of individuals eager to continue the progress we’ve made.”</p><p>But he has not decided whether to forge ahead with a battle for reelection, or to walk away after a single term and avoid having voters potentially push him into political retirement.</p><p>“I’m kind of emotional today because my son is headed off tomorrow. I wish I could just hold on to him a little bit longer. There are parents across this country who have experienced it or will experience it. You just want to hold on to something a little bit longer because you know that once you let go, it will forever change,” the mayor said, his voice breaking.</p><p>“I just want to hold on to the city of Chicago a little bit longer just so that, when the politics come, we will have fully embraced the moment that we’re in.”</p><p></p><p>Chicago now has its lowest homicide rate in 60 years, and the city is gearing up to build more affordable housing. </p><p>“I want to hold on to that a little bit longer," Johnson said. "Because you all know that once there’s an absolute decision that’s made, then it’s Chicago. ... As much as I know I’m gonna have to let go of my son … at some point, I’m gonna have to let go and make a decision. But in the meantime, I have at least another 36 hours with my son." </p><p>With only $631,309 in his campaign fund compared to nearly $22 million for Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, Johnson is leaning heavily on social media and the power of incumbency — along with the free media that comes with it. That strategy was on full display at Tuesday’s City Hall news conference.</p><p>For senior citizens affected by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/25/shoppers-left-stranded-as-save-a-lot-grocery-stores-permanently-close-we-have-to-eat-too" >Yellow Banana grocery store closings,</a> Johnson announced that a $25,000 grant from Lyft would offer seniors free round-trip rides to grocery stores.</p><p>The city, which invested $13 million in the now-shuttered Yellow Banana stores, continues to explore “additional pathways to improve food security, including public markets and other innovative models that expand access to fresh, affordable food while creating opportunities for local entrepreneurs,” Johnson said.</p><p>The mayor also announced 2,000 “additional paid summer job opportunities” for young people “during these critical final weeks,” along with preapprenticeship skills training and job placement services for 1,500 young adults between the ages of 18 and 24.</p><p></p><p>Before driving his son to Eastern Illinois University to begin his first year, Johnson reflected on the $639.6 million migrant crisis he inherited, the difficult choices that it forced him to make, and the political price he paid for those decisions reigniting an us-versus-them conflict between Blacks and Hispanics.</p><p> </p><p>"I understand the frustration that Black people felt during that mission." I do. I do,” Johnson said, pausing to gather himself. “Here’s what I understand: We don’t ask for much. We don’t. We just don’t want our schools to close. We want opportunities for paid jobs. … For Black Chicago in particular, it kind of felt [like] government was able to turn on resources in a moment’s notice — and our communities have been starved for decades.” </p><p>Johnson said he “made a commitment to respond to the most vulnerable” and delivered by moving 3,000 migrants off the floors of Chicago’s district police stations.</p><p>“I tried desperately to live in my values, even though it cost me politically. It did cost me,” he said, accusing the media of misreporting city spending without acknowledging that state funding used to put migrants in hotels was withdrawn when it “got too expensive.”</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Sources said Johnson’s own polling shows his public approval rating among Black voters plunging to 28% in early 2024. It now stands somewhere between 48% and 52% in those same polls.</p><p></p><p>Johnson said there is "no perfect model" for how to "govern as a progressive in the midst of decades of malfeasance and neglect."</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p> </p><p>He added it’s “too soon to prognosticate what the future will hold, but what I can say is that building a safe and affordable city in America is the joy of my experience in this moment.”</p>

entries.title: Bears DE Montez Sweat put on Non-Football Illness List
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will open <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/07/28/bears-training-camp-ryan-poles-kyler-gordon-halas-intrigue-podcast" target="_blank" >training camp</a> Wednesday morning without their best defensive end.</p><p>The team put Montez Sweat on the Active/Non-Football Illness list Tuesday with a short-term illness that is expected to cost him the first few days of camp.</p><p>Sweat had perhaps his best season with the Bears last season, totaling 10 regular season sacks and 18 quarterback hits. He combined for one sack and four quarterback hits in the Bears’ two playoff games. He was ranked 91st on the NFL Top 100 this month.</p><p>“I’d like to see him continue to improve and take what he did last year and add to that,” Bears general manager Ryan Poles said Tuesday, the day Bears veterans reported to training camp.</p><p>Players were subject to physicals upon their return. Safety Elijah Hicks was put on the Physically Unable to Perform list after feeling shin pain. Poles said Hicks’ injury will “take a little bit of time.”</p><p>On Saturday, the Bears put linebacker T.J. Edwards on the Non-Football Injury list after he hurt his right calf training off-site. Poles said it was not a major injury.</p><p>Rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott, who was put on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a back problem, is running and likely to be back soon, the GM said. Poles didn’t have timetables for the return of linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles tendon) , offensive lineman Ozzy Trapilo (patellar tendon) and defensive lineman Shemar Turner (torn ACL), who are all entries.title: Delia Ramírez tilda de devastadoras las condiciones de detenidos de Chicago en centro de ICE de Kentucky
entries.summary: <p>La representante estadounidense Delia Ramírez fue una de las tres legisladoras demócratas que visitaron el lunes un centro de detención del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) en Kentucky para verificar la situación de dos habitantes de Chicago que aseguran no recibir atención médica adecuada para tratar la diabetes, incluyendo un hombre que está detenido desde septiembre.</p><p>Ramírez le dijo al Sun-Times que se fue "con más preguntas y más preocupaciones" que cuando entró y calificó las condiciones en la cárcel del condado convertida en centro de detención como "devastadoras". El centro tiene capacidad para 129 detenidos de ICE mientras que el resto de las instalaciones alberga a la población general de la cárcel. Ramírez dijo que el lunes el centro estaba al máximo con 430 reclusos y detenidos.</p><p>La congresista por Illinois se unió a la visita al Centro de Detención del Condado de Campbell, en Newport, Kentucky, junto a la representante Gwen Moore, demócrata por Wisconsin, y al representante Morgan McGarvey, demócrata por Kentucky, donde verificó el estado de dos detenidos: Ricardo, un hombre de 39 años detenido desde septiembre, y Octavio, de 53 años, detenido desde hace dos meses. Ramírez dijo que ambos son diabéticos y se han quejado ante ella por la comida y la medicación insuficientes.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e90000" name="module-e90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Es devastador, de verdad", contó Ramírez tras su visita. "Tengo dos detenidos que son diabéticos y no están recibiendo su insulina; en su lugar les dan medicación para la prediabetes porque no les quieren dar insulina. Al mismo tiempo, la comida está vencida y todo es pasta, arroz y alimentos con muchos carbohidratos. Así no tienen que darles una comida realmente balanceada con proteínas. Uno de ellos no ha comido carne en seis meses porque se cansó de comer carne de res con gusanos y caducada. Siempre están enfermos".</p><p>El Sun-Times contactó al Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) para preguntar por la atención médica y la dieta de ambos hombres. DHS solicitó más información sobre ambos detenidos, incluidos sus nombres completos, fechas de nacimiento y números de registro de 9 dígitos, pero no hizo comentarios de inmediato. El Sun-Times proporcionó nombres, edades y países de origen.</p><p>Después de que los miembros del Congreso hablaran con reporteros, el alcalde del Condado de Campbell, James Daley, negó las acusaciones de que a las personas en el centro no se les da acceso a necesidades básicas como atención médica y opciones de comida apta para diabéticos, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wvxu.org/local-news/2026-07-27/lawmakers-campbell-county-jail-are-treated-as-commodities" target="_blank" >según la emisora de radio pública de Cincinnati, WVXU</a>. La cárcel del condado es una de las cientos que tienen un contrato con ICE, un acuerdo que les paga a las cárceles locales por alojar a inmigrantes en detención.</p><p>"Me pagan por retener reclusos de otros condados", dijo Daley a WVXU después de que los representantes se hubieran marchado. "Me pagan por retener reclusos para el estado y por retener reclusos del gobierno federal".</p><p>Ramírez destacó que Ricardo también le contó que no ha salido al exterior desde que ingresó a la instalación en septiembre, salvo por un "tiempo de recreación al aire libre" que él describió como una sala lo suficientemente grande como para que 20 personas estén de pie.</p><p>"Lo que llaman actividades al aire libre es porque hay un par de pequeñas rejillas. Hay rejillas en el techo donde puedes mirar para ver si hoy salió el sol", detalló Ramírez. "Piensen en la inestabilidad mental de las personas que han estado detenidas. No saben cuándo será la próxima fecha de la corte, por qué el juez no se presentó, por qué no tienen debido proceso, por qué se les negó el hábeas corpus".</p><p>Ramírez dijo que la permanencia de 11 meses de Ricardo en el centro se debe a demoras en los procedimientos judiciales.</p><p>"Las cortes están cancelando audiencias. Le han negado su hábeas corpus", dijo Ramírez. "Estamos volviendo a presentar el hábeas por él. Es un camino largo".</p><p>Ramírez también contó que otros detenidos gritaron pidiendo ayuda mientras el grupo visitante se preparaba para salir.</p><p>"Gritaron mientras nos íbamos, 'Por favor, ayúdennos'. Nos tratan muy mal. No nos dan de comer'", dijo Ramírez. "Y este es el clamor de personas que creen que van a morir en detención y que nadie los está vigilando, por eso estas visitas del Congreso son tan increíblemente importantes. Cada miembro debe realizar estas visitas a todos sus constituyentes".</p><p>Los tres miembros del Congreso dijeron que presentarán una carta congresional al DHS exigiendo una respuesta inmediata, y Ramírez dijo que quiere saber, para el martes, si sus constituyentes están recibiendo su insulina.</p><p>"Si tengo que volver aquí, voy a volver", destacó Ramírez.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bogus meds seized at O’Hare includes drugs for ED, weight loss
entries.summary: <p>Customs agents at O’Hare Airport on Tuesday announced the seizure of a massive shipment of “unapproved medications” from China that included erectile dysfunction and weight-loss drugs.</p><p>The shipment destined for Syracuse, New York, was intercepted by a U.S. Customs and Border Protection team at O’Hare, the agency said in a statement.</p><p>It contained 10,412 tablets and 2,144 vials of bogus medications, human growth hormones and steroids, according to the statement. Most alarming, the seizure included “various unapproved medications used to treat serious medical conditions like cancer, thyroid disorders, and breathing illnesses.”</p><p>Smugglers tried to sneak the medications into the country using “a master carton smuggling scheme, wherein a single shipment contains many smaller, unmanifested, individual shipments,” customs officials said.</p><p>“The illegal importation of unsafe or unregulated prescription drugs like these are known to pose a significant risk to patients and consumers,” said Michael Pfeiffer, acting director of field operations for CBP’s Chicago office.</p>

entries.title: Bears' Ben Johnson, Ryan Poles tell all — with a little help from a translator — on eve of training camp
entries.summary: <p>You probably knew this already, but it’s Caleb Williams’ second year of playing quarterback for Ben Johnson. And Dennis Allen’s second year of running the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defense for Johnson. And Ryan Poles’ second year of trying to give Johnson whatever he wants. And Bears fans’ second year of bowing at Johnson’s feet.</p><p>What’s not to love about Johnson, who led the Bears to an 11-6 season as a 38-year-old rookie head coach, won a division title and beat the Packers twice, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/10/bears-grades-packers-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-nfc-wild-card-nfc-postseason" target="_blank" >including in a playoff matchup at Soldier Field</a>?</p><p>If there’s one thing Beardom would agree on as training camp gets underway, it’s that Johnson has his end of things locked down.</p><p>But does he? Is he really that far along in his own evolution as a head coach?</p><p>“Still feels like I’m drinking out of a fire hose, if that’s what you mean,” he said Tuesday at Halas Hall.</p><p>There’s still a heck of a lot coming at him and he’s just trying to keep up with it all, in other words. No extra charge for the translation.</p><p>Think about it, though: Johnson is in Year 2 at this. Compared with the Vikings’ Kevin O’Connell (Year 5), the Lions’ Dan Campbell (Year 6) and the Packers’ Matt LaFleur (Year 8), he’s still wet behind the ears, a greenhorn, the Carolina Kid. The division’s other coaches know a thing or two about a thing or two and are looking to knock the Bears and their intense, occasionally shirtless and profane hotshot of a coach down at least a peg. Johnson, better than anybody, must know it.</p><p>On the eve of camp practice No. 1, general manager Poles and Johnson took on questions and delivered answers that verged on the vaguely illuminating, hinted at truths and in some cases required — begged for, even — an expert’s translation.</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“You guys will notice we’ve got two brand-new [practice fields], totally re-sodded.” — Poles</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“I can’t believe I’m saying this, but it might be even nicer here than it is in Hammond, Indiana. By the way, please don’t mention the words ‘stadium fiasco,’ especially not while Kevin Warren is sitting right here in this room. It’s kind of a sore subject.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“[Year 2] is a chance for us to create a new chapter of Bears football.” — Johnson</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“Look, I wouldn’t mind a redo of the last chapter, either, but anybody who thinks we’re going to rally like maniacs to win a jillion games in the fourth quarter again really doesn’t know how this whole NFL thing works.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“It’s important to have that mindset that you’re always hunting. … We’re going to be hunting [as opposed to being the hunted] at all times.” — Poles</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“I'm not sure we can go back-to-back in this division, either, but have I mentioned the freshly sodded practice fields?”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“[Williams] has that ability to put on the Superman cape when the time calls for it.” — Johnson</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“You know what I’m already sick of? Needing that freakin’ cape all the time because we’re always losing. Sure, we had six fourth-quarter comebacks to win last season, and a seventh in the playoffs, but Tom Brady averaged exactly two of them over his career, right around the same as Peyton Manning, Drew Brees, John Elway, Dan Marino, Joe Montana … I could go on, but I’m out of breath.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“[Left tackle] is going to be a great competition.” — Poles</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“Did I forget to go get a top guy at one of the most important positions on the field? My bad.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“I really expect another layer of sophistication to occur within this building and with our players.” — Johnson</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“I will literally gnaw the face off of anyone who slows us down.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“If there’s a guy that I’m really excited about, it’s [wide receiver] Luther Burden. … You can feel the fire inside of him.” — Poles</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“OK, so there’s some diva potential. And you know what? We’re here for it.”</p><p><b>What he said: </b>“Now we’re at the point where [Williams] isn’t thinking about the play call, he’s not thinking about the cadence, the motion and all the ‘jigamarow’ before the snap.” — Johnson</p><p><b>What he meant: </b>“That’s right, I said ‘jigamarow.’ If you don’t know what that means by now, I can’t help you.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/28/bears-coach-ben-johnson-eager-to-see-qb-caleb-williams-turn-potential-into-consistency-in-training-camp" >Bears’ Ben Johnson sends clear message to QB Caleb Williams about completion percentage: Target is 70%</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/28/bears-training-camp-kyler-gordon-get-healthy-ben-johnson-ryan-poles-calf-injury-cornerback" >Frustration mounts as Bears tell CB Kyler Gordon to ‘get healthy’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/28/bears-training-camp-montez-sweat-non-football-illness-list-nfl-defensive-end" target="_blank" >Bears DE Montez Sweat put on Non-Football Illness List</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: At least 5 Chicago School Board races to be uncontested as another candidate kicked off ballot
entries.summary: <p>Voters in at least a quarter of Chicago’s school board districts will see only one name on their ballot in November's historic elections as candidates continue to be removed.</p><p>The Chicago Board of Election Commissioners on Tuesday upheld a challenge to the candidacy of Tameka Walton, who had filed to run for the seat in South Side District 10A, leaving the community with incumbent Che "Rhymefest" Smith as the lone candidate. Earlier this month, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/14/five-chicago-school-board-candidates-removed-from-ballot-including-angel-velez-cydney-wallace" >board removed Krista Nichols Alston</a>, the other challenger in that district.</p><p>The decisions leave five uncontested races so far: District 4B on the North Side, 8A and 8B on the Southwest Side and 9A and 10A on the South Side. Two districts had only one candidate to start, while the others became uncontested through successful challenges to candidates’ nominating paperwork.</p><p>But election commissioners have yet to make final decisions on objections to candidates in four districts, three of which have only two people in the running. If those challenges are successful, up to eight of the 20 school board district races this fall could be uncontested — which would leave much of the city with little actual say over who represents them on the first fully elected school board.</p><p>The board on Tuesday also confirmed 10 candidates that faced challenges will appear on November's ballot, including Victor Henderson and Hilario Dominguez, two of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/22/meet-the-candidates-for-chicagos-first-ever-elected-school-board-president" >five people vying for school board president</a>. Now, all five will appear on the ballot.</p><p>A challenge to Dominguez’s candidacy was dismissed after an examination of his paperwork found that 4,172 of the 8,592 signatures he gathered were valid, far exceeding the minimum requirement of 2,500, <a class="Link" href="https://cboeprod.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/prod/2026-07/26-EB-SBP-004%20Findings%20and%20Decision.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>the board found</u></a>. Challenges against Henderson were withdrawn. Challenges against two other presidential candidates, Jessica Biggs and Sendhil Revuluri, were previously withdrawn. No objections were filed against Jennifer Custer.</p><p>The remaining cases should be resolved by mid-August, letting voters know who will be on the final ballot.</p><p>Brenda Lee Anderson, who teaches at Northwestern University, was among the candidates able to fend off a challenge. The board dismissed objections to her signatures on Tuesday.</p><p>As a newcomer in the school board race, Anderson said it was disheartening to learn that two people contested her paperwork after she spent weeks walking around her district to gather signatures. Anderson described the objections process as unfair and said it’s part of the political process that discourages broader community involvement.</p><p>“People will come up to me like, ‘Oh, this is just a part of the Chicago process, you have to challenge people’s petitions,” Anderson said. “And I said, ‘no.’”</p><p>She didn’t have money for an attorney to defend her, so she took up the Chicago Teachers Union’s offer to provide free legal support to candidates without attorneys.</p><p>“I’m frustrated because this is exhausting,” Anderson said.</p><p>But not everyone has been able to fight off challenges. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/14/five-chicago-school-board-candidates-removed-from-ballot-including-angel-velez-cydney-wallace" >Elections commissioners have removed</a> six candidates from the ballot so far. That includes two incumbents: Angel Velez, who represents District 9A on the Southwest Side and is the board vice president, and Cydney Wallace, who represents District 8B on the South Side.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/04/half-of-chicago-school-board-candidates-are-facing-challenges-but-powerful-ctu-says-it-didnt-file-any" >More than half of the 51 candidates</a> that filed paperwork to run for a seat on the board faced challenges. Each case is treated like a mini-trial with both sides presenting evidence before the board makes a final decision.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/14/five-chicago-school-board-candidates-removed-from-ballot-including-angel-velez-cydney-wallace" >5 school board candidates removed from ballot, including 2 incumbents</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/04/half-of-chicago-school-board-candidates-are-facing-challenges-but-powerful-ctu-says-it-didnt-file-any" >Half of Chicago school board candidates are facing challenges</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/26/51-candidates-are-running-for-chicagos-first-fully-elected-school-board" >51 candidates are running for Chicago’s first fully elected school board</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: With pitching obvious trade-deadline focus, are Cubs getting best version of David Peterson at right time?
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS — When David Peterson served up a solo homer in the second inning Monday night, it looked like a continuation of a potentially worrisome trend.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ lefty starter arrived in a midseason trade with a reputation as an elite ground-ball pitcher, and given the Gold Glove defenders populating the infield, it seemed like a perfect fit, the right ingredients for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/26/cubs-david-peterson-trade-mets-starting-rotation-craig-counsell-all-star-pitcher" >a change-of-scenery success story</a> after Peterson, a 2025 All Star, saw his fortunes dip with the Mets.</p><p>But since coming to the Cubs, his ground-ball numbers hadn’t been nearly as good as they were with his former team. He took a 32.4% ground-ball rate into his fifth start as a Cub on Monday, which paled in comparison to the 51.1% rate he had in 16 appearances with the Mets.</p><p>And then the home run, the fourth he’d allowed in five outings after giving up just six in 16 pre-trade appearances.</p><p>But it wasn’t a harbinger of doom. Instead, Peterson turned in his best performance since the trade, getting more grounders than fly balls for the first time since changing uniforms.</p><p>“David pitched really, really well,” manager Craig Counsell said after the game. “I obviously haven’t seen a lot of David when he was at his best, but this — the ground balls, the swings at the sinker — feels like this is what it looks like. It was good to see.</p><p>“You see the ground balls starting to go up, and that’s exactly what we want.”</p><p>Getting the best version of Peterson — whose ground-ball rate ticked up to 36.5% after Monday’s winning effort — would be a big development for a Cubs team still battling depth issues on a staff that’s been ravaged by injuries and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/27/cubs-jameson-taillon-dfa-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-rotation" >just cut loose veteran righty Jameson Taillon</a> due to poor performance.</p><p>Peterson has been very effective in four of the five starts he’s made with the Cubs, with a 1.96 ERA in those four outings. His overall numbers are enlarged thanks to a clunker against this same Cardinals team in which he gave up 10 runs and didn’t make it through four innings.</p><p>Monday, Peterson was the kind of pitcher the Cubs hoped they’d see when they made the trade, the type of pitcher he was during the 2024 campaign — he finished that season with a 2.90 ERA — and the first half of last season, which featured a 2.49 ERA in his first 13 starts and culminated in that trip to the All-Star Game.</p><p>“It was good to go out there and execute,” Peterson said. “Some of the things that we’ve been working on continued to click even more [Monday], and they’re getting better and better and more normal every time I go out.</p><p>“It’s definitely a lot closer to ‘24 and early ‘25, but I don’t necessarily look at it that way. The performances are closer to that, but I’m focused on being a better version of myself every day. That’s the goal.”</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office figures to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >make more trades for pitching</a> over the next several days ahead of Monday’s trade deadline. Fans are hoping there’s a big, splashy deal in there somewhere, but no matter <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" >how aggressive Hoyer & Co. get</a>, the pitching staff figures to look different come Tuesday.</p><p>After Taillon’s departure, lefties Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga are the entrenched duo at the top of the rotation, and they’ve been pitching like it. Righties Colin Rea and Javier Assad — the latter will, at least briefly, slot into Taillon’s vacated rotation spot — started the season in the bullpen and are capable of heading back there, should Hoyer add pitchers that force such a move.</p><p>Peterson, though, figures to stay where he is. And if he can deliver like he did Monday, that will go a long way to lengthening a rotation that dealt with depth issues during its briefer-than-hoped playoff stay last fall.</p><p>“He was outstanding,” third baseman Alex Bregman said of Peterson. “For me, that was the best I’ve seen him here, so far, and he’s going to continue to do that on a really consistent basis.”</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Libertyville man gets 6 months in prison for threatening federal judges with photos of bullets
entries.summary: <p>Soon after sentencing began Tuesday<b> </b>for<b> </b>a<b> </b>north suburban<b> </b>man<b> </b>who<b> </b>threatened<b> </b>two<b> </b>federal<b> </b>judges<b> </b>with letters<b> </b>containing pictures of bullets, it became clear that U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis<b> </b>would not spare him from prison.</p><p>She told James Lebuhn that it’s one thing for an individual<b> </b>to take on the risk and obligation of becoming a judge. It’s another to have to “look your kid in the eye”<b> </b>and say “your home is not safe.”</p><p>So while Lebuhn insisted he’d made a one-time mistake, Ellis said she had “to think about the people that are sitting in front of their computer who are angry and frustrated and feel like they don’t have a voice, and they feel like the world is going in a direction they don’t agree with.”</p><p>Then she gave Lebuhn<b> </b>six months<b> </b>in prison, reminding<b> </b>the<b> </b>66-year-old<b> </b>Libertyville<b> </b>man<b> </b>that<b> </b>“if we allow folks to just do what they want and threaten people in order to get the outcome that they want, that will ruin democracy faster really than anything we can do.”</p><p>The sentencing comes as concern continues to rise about threats to judges, with U.S. Supreme Court Justice Amy<b> </b>Coney<b> </b>Barrett<b> </b>testifying<b> </b>just weeks ago<b> </b>about<b> </b>having to explain to her 12-year-old son<b> </b>why<b> </b>she’d come home<b> </b>with a bulletproof vest.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/20/judge-in-bovino-murder-plot-case-warned-of-threats-to-judges-after-family-members-were-killed-in-2005" >Judge in Bovino murder-plot case warned of threats to judiciary after her family members were killed in 2005</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lebuhn<b> </b>pleaded guilty<b> </b>in March<b> </b>to<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/12/libertyville-man-accused-sending-threatening-letters-to-federal-judges" target="_blank" >sending<b> </b>threatening letters</a> on March 24, 2025, admitting<b> </b>he’d<b> </b>also<b> </b>sent<b> </b>them to<b> </b>employees<b> </b>of the Office of Personnel Management<b> </b>in Washington, D.C. </figure> </div> </div><p> and<b> </b>Fort Pierce, Florida.</p><p>The only judges sitting in those cities are U.S. District Judge Matthew<b> </b>Kacsmaryk of Texas and<b> </b>U.S. District Judge Aileen<b> </b>Cannon<b> </b>of Florida, who were both appointed by President Donald Trump. Cannon presided over Trump’s<b> </b>criminal case<b> </b>involving classified documents.</p><p>Lebuhn<b> </b>sent<b> </b>both judges<b> </b>a letter that read, “the citizens do not like what you are doing to our democracy. They know who you are.” Below those words were pictures of two bullets, followed by the warning, “Be careful. The level of anger is rising.”</p><p>One of the threatened judges listened remotely to Tuesday’s sentencing, Ellis said.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard<b> </b>Rothblatt<b> </b>told Ellis that threats like Lebuhn’s “have impact on real people in their day-to-day life”<b> </b>and<b> </b>“can’t be countenanced by the judicial system or the government writ large.”</p><p>Later, Lebuhn told Ellis, “I feel very ashamed about what I’ve done.”<b> </b>His attorney, Steve<b> </b>Dollear, wrote in a court filing that Lebuhn “broke under personal and family stress and acted out” by making the threats in what was “the lowest moment in his life.”</p><p>Dollear said Lebuhn lost his job<b> </b>as a financial analyst<b> </b>and wound up taking a job as a bus driver. He confessed in separate interviews with the Federal Protective Service, the U.S. Marshal Service and U.S. Postal Service,<b> </b>and the U.S. Secret Service, the attorney wrote.</p><p>Dollear sought a sentence of probation during Tuesday’s hearing. But Ellis told him, “in a case like this involving threats to government employees and officials … you have an uphill battle to convince me that probation is appropriate.”</p><div class="Enhancement" </figure> </div> </div><p>The government employees threatened by Lebuhn weren’t entitled to the same level of protection given to judges, Ellis noted. So for them, “this was an even more frightening experience,” she said.</p><p>“They can’t turn to the Secret Service or the Marshals Service for protection,” Ellis said. “They just have to hope against hope that they’ll be safe at work. Or safe at home.”</p><p>Security concerns prevent<b> </b>U.S. District Court officials from discussing specific threats faced by judges in Chicago, court spokesman Sean<b> </b>Lewis<b> </b>told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“The fair administration of justice, the rule of law and the safety and security of our judges and entire court family are among our highest priorities,” he said.</p><p>Still, individual judges have not been shy about the threats they’ve faced. U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman said she’d been “called almost every kind of name in the book” as she sentenced<b> </b>a man<b> </b>to more than three years in prison<b> </b>this month<b> </b>for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/07/08/president-donald-trump-trent-schneider-sharon-johnson-coleman-chicago" target="_blank" >threatening Trump<b> </b>and others</a>.</p><p>The 2005 murder<b> </b>of<b> </b>U.S. District Judge Joan Lefkow’s<b> </b>mother and husband<b> </b>by a man Lefkow had ruled against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/20/judge-in-bovino-murder-plot-case-warned-of-threats-to-judges-after-family-members-were-killed-in-2005" target="_blank" >remains fresh in the minds</a> of many at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/07/08/president-donald-trump-trent-schneider-sharon-johnson-coleman-chicago" >Suburban Chicago man gets 3 years in prison for saying Trump, others ‘should all be executed’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Ellis also presided<b> </b>last fall<b> </b>over <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/21/judge-hands-down-critical-review-of-federal-immigration-agents-unprecedented-use-of-force" target="_blank" >a high-profile legal challenge</a><b> </b>to Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign in Chicago. During one hearing in the case, she said, “I can’t tell you how many judges have received death threats.”</p><p>“It’s unfortunately part of the cost of doing business as a public servant in the government,” Ellis said then. “That, unfortunately, society has devolved to the point where anyone who disagrees with how you do your job is subjected to threats.”</p><p>Ellis<b> </b>and<b> </b>Coleman<b> </b>were both appointed to the bench by President Barack Obama. A colleague of theirs, U.S. District Judge April Perry,<b> </b>also acknowledged receiving threats last fall. They came as Perry, appointed<b> </b>by<b> </b>President Joe Biden, grappled with whether to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/04/20/trump-chicago-national-guard-midway-blitz-crime" target="_blank" >block Trump’s deployment of National Guard troops</a> into Illinois. She eventually did so.</p><p>But before she ruled, she told a Trump administration lawyer, “I agree with you about the seriousness of threats generally across the United States right now.</p><p>“I don’t think there is a single public servant, really, who is not being subjected to threats,” Perry told him.</p><p>“Mine started about 10 minutes after I got this case.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago needs to change tactics in war on rats, IG says
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Inspector General David Glockner may have found the reason why the city has the dubious distinction of consistently showing up on Orkin’s list of the nation’s “rattiest cities.”</p><p>The Department of Streets and Sanitation’s poison-based approach to “reports of rat sightings and infestations” fails to “target sources of food and shelter” that allow the rodent population to soar, Glockner said.</p><p>Instead of throwing poison at the problem, Chicago needs a “unified strategy coordinated across city departments to cut rats off from the resources that let them thrive and multiply." </p><p>Without a change in tactics, it will be nearly impossible to make lasting progress, and Chicagoans will “continue to face fresh crops of rats," he said.</p><p>“While Chicago has a team that’s working hard on this issue, the particular strategy that we’re using is an approach that’s probably best described as very reactive,” Glockner told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“A more strategic approach that focuses on getting rid of the sources of food, shelter — the things that rats really need to thrive and multiply — is in the long term much more likely to be effective. If all you’re doing is essentially responding to complaints and deploying rodenticide or poison, you’re not dealing with the long-term causes of the problem, and it’s just going to recur.”</p><p>Glockner promised during his May 19 confirmation hearing to focus the inspector general’s audit work on “areas that matter most” and have the greatest potential to minimize risk, save the cash-strapped city money, and deliver city services more equitably and efficiently.</p><p>The rodent control audit fills the bill.</p><p>It advises the city’s third-largest department to use a “surveying approach to collect and monitor” the data it collects on a range of factors that support rat populations, including “garbage and alley conditions, active rat signs such as burrow holes, nearby vacant lots, green space, restaurant inspections” and building code violations.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/07/17/rat-birth-control-pilot-program-coming-to-lincoln-park" >Rat birth control pilot program coming to Lincoln Park</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Streets and Sanitation Commissioner Cole Stallard was further advised to “establish thresholds at which rat activity or root causes warrant intervention to prevent infestation,” prioritize and coordinate city services to “deliver nontoxic interventions … before using poison as a last resort,” and create a policy for the safe use of pesticides and "train employees on the circumstances that warrant the use of poison.”</p><p>Glockner said he chose rodent control as the subject of one of his earliest audits because rats are “vectors of disease, can cause bites and it is a struggle that cities across the world face.” </p><p>“You can put the poison down. But if you don’t get rid of the food sources and don’t deal with debris or brush or infrastructure that may provide harboring spots for rats, all you’re doing is briefly knocking them back — and they’re gonna come back and rebound,” he said.</p><p>Breaking down bureaucratic walls between city departments to forge a coordinated strategy “takes effort and time, but it doesn’t have to cost extra money,” Glockner said.</p><p>Stallard said he recently launched a massive public education campaign, with advertising on CTA buses and trains and digital ads at O’Hare and Midway airports that urge Chicagoans to stop throwing trash on the street and to pick up after their dogs.</p><p>But even after holding 200 community meetings each of the last two years to spread the word, Stallard acknowledged that there is “room for improvement” in his department’s approach to rodent control.</p><p>“We use rodenticide, which they kept referencing as poison. It is rodenticide. It is EPA-approved. But we understand the message. They’re going after the integrated pest management. We like to say we do it. Maybe not up to perfect standard. There’s definitely room for improvement,” Stallard said Tuesday.</p><p>Chicago’s $12.5 million-a-year Rodent Control Bureau has 107 employees, not all of them working directly on rodent abatement. The staff includes four administrators and employees who deliver garbage and recycling carts.</p><p>Stallard said the key to controlling Chicago’s exploding rat population is to starve the rodents by convincing people to stop littering and pressure dog owners to clean up after their dogs.</p><p>“If I throw Chicago’s finest New York steak down in an alley and someone doesn’t pick up after their dog, the rodents are … walking over that steak to get to the dog feces,” the commissioner said.</p><p>Stallard said his employees “clean up 60,000 bags of litter a year” on streets and sidewalks.</p><p></p><p>Stallard was skeptical about turning his employees into what he called the "poop police" by fining dog owners who don't clean up after their pets. </p><p>"Try to catch somebody not picking up after their dog. It may be a challenge to enforce that," he said.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson's acting CFO abruptly departs as budget season looms
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is losing his chief financial officer just as Chicago prepares to host a crucial investors conference and an emboldened City Council gears up for a grueling election-year budget season.</p><p>Acting Chief Financial Officer Steven Mahr replaced Jill Jaworski, who left City Hall in January for a job at Navy Pier shortly after a renegade City Council majority rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative city budget with major elements Johnson continues to battle.</p><p>Now, Mahr is also leaving after less than eight months as Jaworski’s interim replacement. </p><p>For Wall Street rating agencies and investors soon to arrive in Chicago for the annual investors conference, Mahr's departure could signal a level of instability — with an embattled mayor at the helm, facing an uphill battle for a second term if he chooses to seek reelection, and a City Council more independent than it has ever been.</p><p>Chicago is facing a $90 million midyear budget shortfall, with a $1 billion-plus hole in next year’s budget and a $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p>Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd), chair of the City Council’s Finance Committee, said Mahr “stepped into a big job” when Jaworski left, was “really good at explaining complex finances” and took “tons of shots for the administration when they basically hung him out to dry during hearings” before the City Council.</p><p>His departure is “bad timing considering that the budget process is beginning,” Dowell said.</p><p>“When you step into a position like that and you’re fairly junior, you need to have support, and I’m not sure he had that,” Dowell told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Asked whether it was Budget Direct Annette Guzman who pulled the rug out from under Mahr, Dowell said, “Who is more senior? I couldn’t even point to somebody.”</p><p>Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) added, “It’s become apparent to me that the budget director doesn’t play well with others in the sandbox. And we need a budget director, a comptroller and a chief financial officer working together.”</p><p>The tension between Guzman and Mahr was on full display during a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/16/chicago-city-hall-pension-advance-payment-delay-cfo-steve-mahr" >City Council hearing </a>earlier this month on the city’s midyear financial report.</p><p>After Guzman set the stage by citing late property tax payments from Cook County, Mahr said he was in the process of evaluating when the city could afford to make the second half of a $260 million advance pension payment that was at the center of the budget battle and, if so, how much that additional payment would be.</p><p>“Cook County indicated a few weeks ago that property taxes are likely to be delayed by about two months. Now that we have this news about Cook County property tax delays coming again this year, we are continuing the analysis to determine when and in what amount we will make the second installment of the supplemental pension payment,” Mahr said at the hearing.</p><p>Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) reminded Mahr that restoring the full $260 million pension advance was “one of the driving forces behind the budget battle last December” adding, “It’s not gonna go away. The promise that we made to our workforce isn’t gonna go away.”</p><p>Mahr said he was “acutely aware” of how important it is to Wall Street rating agencies to continue to make those advance payments.</p><p>“My goal, my commitment is to figuring out when we can make that payment in the context of all of the other things going on," he said.</p><p>Mahr could not be reached for comment. Sources said he is leaving without having landed another job. </p><p>“Being under that circus tent for eight months — he’s got a career ahead of him. He’s an impressive young man. I would suspect that he just got fed up with these folks,” O’Shea said. “Fed up with no clear plan. Fed up with mixed messages. Fed up with absolutely no communication at a time when, now more than ever, city leadership needs to be working together on a cohesive plan to get us out of the financial predicament that we’re in.”</p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson said what’s more concerning than the reasons for Mahr’s abrupt exit is the timing of his departure.</p><p>The CFO normally serves as “primary speaker to the investment community” at the annual investors conference, which is next month.</p><p>“Last year, it was Jill Jaworski. This year, it appears that we’ll be headed into the investors conference without a [permanent] CFO. That is a very bad signal to the community,” Ferguson said.</p><p>A City Council that already lacks confidence in the Johnson administration's revenue estimates and recommendations on "levels of, and structuring of, debt" will have less faith in those statements, further complicating the budget season, Ferguson said.</p>

entries.title: Southern chef and cookbook author Vivian Howard embraces okra and aims to change minds with her recipes
entries.summary: <p>If the South had a mascot, it would be okra. You love, hate or have an unfounded fear of okra — and the same is true of the South.</p><p>There’s no vegetable more polarizing than this poor little pod. And it’s only one part of okra that tends to bother people: the slimy seeds. Now I seek okra out. I want to cook with it. I want to change people’s minds about it. I’m not going to print myself an “I Love Okra” T-shirt or name my next child after it, but I understand and respect it just as much as I do every other vegetable.</p><p>These fritters from my cookbook “Deep Run Roots” capitalize on okra's slime like nothing else. They’re sort of a cross between a scallion pancake and fried okra, and their pillowy texture and vegetal flavor, coupled with the sweet pop of corn, is pleasing and addictive.</p><p>Choose large mature pods, and use only their fat midsections. The swollen seeds hiding in there will actually do a lot to hold the fritter batter together. I like to eat these fritters right out of the frying pan over stewed tomatoes, but they’re also nice at room temperature as a scoop for hummus.</p><h3>Summer Vegetable Scallion Pancakes</h3><p>Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>1 cup okra, caps and tips removed, midsections minced<br>½ cup fresh corn, cut off the cob<br>¼ cup squash or zucchini, grated on a box grater or in a food processor<br>3 tablespoons minced scallion<br>1 teaspoon salt, divided<br>2 tablespoons cornmeal<br>2 tablespoons all-purpose flour<br>2 tablespoons buttermilk<br>1 egg<br>¼ teaspoon hot sauce<br>¼ to ⅓ cup vegetable oil</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Preheat your oven to 200°F. In a medium bowl, stir together the minced okra, corn, squash, scallion, and ½ teaspoon of the salt. Let that sit for about 5 minutes. The salt will leach out the moisture in the squash. That moisture will activate the slime in the okra and bring the veggies together in kind of a gooey-looking mass.</p><p>Stir in the cornmeal and flour to incorporate. Whisk together the buttermilk, egg and hot sauce, and stir it into the dry, slimy mass. Mix this up a few times and let it sit at least 3 minutes and up to 1 hour before you get ready to cook the fritters.</p><p>In a 10- to 12-inch skillet or cast-iron pan, add the oil over medium heat. If you want larger fritters, spoon about 2 tablespoons of the batter into the preheated oil and press down on each dollop to flatten it slightly. The fritters should be about ¼ inch thick. If you'd like smaller fritters, start with 1 tablespoon of batter.</p><p>Carefully continue dropping dollops of batter into the hot oil, making sure the fritters don't touch. Cook the fritters over medium heat on each side till they are chestnut-colored in some spots and golden in others. Transfer the fritters to a paper-towel-lined plate to drain and season them while hot with the remaining salt. Keep them warm in your oven while you fry the next batch.</p><p>Serve warm.<br>___</p><p>Vivian Howard is the chef and owner of the acclaimed Chef and the Farmer restaurant in Kinston, North Carolina. The first woman since Julia Child to win a Peabody Award for a cooking program, she co-created and stars in the PBS series “A Chef's Life.”</p><p>Excerpted from “Deep Run Roots” by Vivian Howard. Copyright (copyright) 2016 by Vivian Howard. Used with permission of Voracious, an imprint of Little, Brown and Company. New York, NY. All rights reserved.</p>

entries.title: As Illinois House Speaker Emanuel 'Chris' Welch navigates a new crisis, an older scandal remains unresolved
entries.summary: <p>When Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch was first elected to the powerful legislative position in 2021, the National Organization for Women’s Chicago chapter raised concerns over accusations he had engaged in domestic violence and sexual harassment years earlier, saying they were serious enough to warrant some kind of investigation.</p><p>That echoed remarks at the time from state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, who, according to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" >published reports</a>, said: “It is my fervent wish that these allegations will be vigorously reviewed so that we can move forward as a unified caucus embracing this historic moment.”</p><p>But five years later — as new questions emerge about whether Welch slow-walked sexual harassment accusations brought against now-former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/03/plainfield-state-rep-harry-benton-resigns-amid-allegations-of-misconduct" >state Rep. Harry Benton, </a>D-Plainfield — there is no indication any such investigation ever occurred.</p><p>Said one person familiar with the situation: “I don’t think it was ever spoken of again.”</p><p>If that’s the case, it’s unclear why.</p><p>Welch’s government spokesman Jon Maxson said it was news to him if there was ever talk in 2021 about an investigation into this “very old story,” but he said he would check into it. He never got back to a reporter.</p><p>Cassidy declined to comment, and officials from NOW couldn’t be reached.</p><p>But as Welch finds himself facing a new crisis, an apparent lack of any investigation in the five years since the 2021 speaker election seems to indicate the old crisis was never fully resolved.</p><p>A 2002 suburban police report alleged that Welch slammed his girlfriend’s head into a countertop during an argument, though he was never criminally charged and has denied wrongdoing. He later said he has “reconciled with the individual since that night. ... Their family lives in my district and are proud supporters of my public service and work.”</p><p>A former school board member of Proviso Township High School District 209, Welch was accused in lawsuits of sexually harassing one female employee there and retaliating against another after she rejected his attempt at a hug, records show. Both cases were later dismissed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dd0000" name="image-dd0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5378c8d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6c298c5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ddebb20/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Part of a 2010 federal lawsuit against Emanuel "Chris" Welch and others before he became Illinois House speaker. The suit was later dismissed." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ddebb20/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ac5a881/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ddebb20/2147483647/strip/true/crop/990x556+0+377/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2F57%2F90ea3ae04f93932f0990a2b140bf%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-28-at-3-30-41-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Part of a 2010 federal lawsuit against Emanuel “Chris” Welch and others before he became Illinois House speaker. The suit was later dismissed.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>U.S. District Court</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A Hillside Democrat, Welch was chosen as speaker after his predecessor and longtime political ally, Michael J. Madigan, was forced out of the post amid a corruption investigation that later saw him charged, convicted and sent to prison.</p><p>Among the schemes outlined by federal prosecutors: Madigan associates helped alleged sexual harasser <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2019/10/2/20885781/madigan-aide-kevin-quinn-sexual-harassment-alaina-hampton-inspector-general-report" >Kevin Quinn,</a> a Madigan political aide, get hired and paid by lobbying firms so he could stay afloat financially after being fired by Madigan’s political operation in the wake of the sexual misconduct accusations.</p><p>Among the lobbyists who helped out Quinn was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/21/lobbyist-will-cousineau-michael-madigan-cornerstone-government-affairs-general-assembly-campaign-donations" target="_blank" >Will Cousineau</a>, whose lobbying firm Cornerstone Government Affairs also helped Welch’s wife during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/2/18/22936193/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-shawnte-raines-al-ronan-kantas-karen-yarbrough-del-galdo" target="_blank" >her successful run for Cook County judge</a> in 2022.</p><p>Benton resigned earlier this month amid unspecified harassment allegations that were deemed “outrageous, unethical, and unbecoming” by Welch, who had booted the two-term lawmaker from Democratic caucus meetings in February pending an investigation by Legislative Inspector General Mike McCuskey.</p><p>Welch and Gov. JB Pritzker both initially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" target="_blank" ><u>cast doubt</u></a> on whether McCuskey’s report could be released under state ethics laws, which have long been derided as toothless by both sides of the aisle.</p><p>But Welch has stood by his handling of the case.</p><p>“I think the process worked,” he said July 6. “I think accountability was had.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure He hasn’t addressed the case other than saying it placed “tremendous strain on my family” and asking for privacy. And he hasn’t given up his $72,000-per-year elected post as Wheatland Township highway commissioner. </p><p>But the case has raised further questions about Welch, who allegedly sent emojis in social has been "trying to cover up and protect the Democrat caucus — but you can't protect your members to the detriment and safety of others."</p><p>"He's not supporting victims" and "at a minimum he entries.title: Devastating Wisconsin tornado stayed on the ground more than 20 minutes
entries.summary: <p>First responders searched homes and buildings on Tuesday for possible victims of a powerful tornado that ravaged several northeastern Wisconsin communities.</p><p>The Fox Cities region, which is home to more than 100,000 people in the communities of Appleton, Menasha and Neenah, was left in shambles by Monday's twister, with homes leveled, cars flipped, and power lines and trees toppled.</p><p>“The depth of the tornado and its impact is incredible, devastating. We’re really still at the assessment stage,” Winnebago County Executive Gordon Hintz said at a news conference Tuesday.</p><p>Authorities said the timing — the storm arrived in the early afternoon, when most people were awake and after warnings had been issued — could be why there have been no reported deaths.</p><p>“Everybody was at work. It was the middle of the day," Menasha Police Chief Matt Albrecht said. "Most people were not at home and at their place of employment.”</p><p>Dozens of people were injured, and officers were still going door-to-door a day later in search of possible victims.</p><p>The tornado touched down around 1 p.m. and remained on the ground for more than 20 minutes, cutting a roughly 12-mile path of destruction, the National Weather Service reported. The area is about 100 miles northwest of Milwaukee.</p><p>It was classified as an EF3 tornado — the strongest to strike Outagamie and Winnebago counties since an EF4 touched down in April 1984, the weather service said.</p><h3>A relatively powerful twister</h3><p>Gov. Tony Evers declared a state of emergency for the affected areas. Shelters were opened for displaced residents.</p><p>As chainsaws roared in the background, Appleton Mayor Jake Woodford said a number of neighborhoods were “truly devastated.” Like elsewhere in the region, electricity lines were tangled around broken trees, making power restoration a slow, risky process.</p><p>More than 10,000 customers in Winnebago and Outagamie counties were still without power Tuesday afternoon, according to utilities that serve them. It could be several days before power is restored.</p><p>The twister was spun off from a large storm system that moved through the Great Lakes and was fueled by a buildup of heat and humidity, the weather service said.</p><p>“What we are seeing this summer is significant heat leading to significant severe weather,” said Chad Merrill, senior meteorologist at AccuWeather. “We had an EF3 tornado in Wisconsin. People need to take these warnings seriously. It can happen just about anywhere.”</p><h3>Residents describe terrifying moments</h3><p>ThedaCare Regional Medical Centers in Appleton and Neenah said they treated 40 people, mostly for minor storm-related injuries. Ascension St. Elizabeth Hospital in Appleton said it saw about 30 patients, all with minor injuries.</p><p>Rachel Bernhardt, 56, said she grabbed her dog and dashed to her basement in the village of Fox Crossing after she saw a steel swing spinning in the yard. After the storm passed, her second-floor bedroom was covered in glass, and a tree branch was resting on her bed.</p><p>“We can’t be in there anymore,” said Bernhardt, who is sleeping on the first floor and using a generator to keep the refrigerator going. “In fact, I’m going to caution-tape that off.”</p><p>At Manderfield’s Home Bakery, a decades-old landmark in Menasha, the brick frame around the door still stood, but not much more.</p><p>“This can be replaced,” owner Jerry Manderfield told WISN-TV. “We had people in the building that could possibly have died in there.”</p><p>Volunteers stepped up to try to ease the shock. Luigi’s Pizza in Menasha set up a food trailer to distribute hygiene packs and free slices after donors kicked in enough money to make at least 125 pizzas.</p><p>“Sometimes a hot pizza, a taco, and a reminder that your community cares can mean more than words,” said Duncan’s Window & Door, which chipped in for 50 pizzas.</p>

entries.title: Sky's Sydney Taylor is not an All-Star yet, but the right people are noticing her
entries.summary: <p>When the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> played the Aces earlier this month, Las Vegas coach Becky Hammon was asked her impression of rookie guard Sydney Taylor.</p><p>Hammon needed only one word to make her point.</p><p>“Stud,” she said.</p><p>It was high praise from the coach of the defending champions. And Hammon isn't the only basketball legend taking notice.</p><p>During All-Star weekend in Chicago, NBA champions Dwyane Wade and Kevin Durant approached Taylor and told her they had noticed her game. </p><p>She's kind of hard to miss. The 5-9 guard has the kind of bounce that once allowed her to dunk a tennis ball and the burst to beat almost anyone off the dribble.</p><p>Taylor went undrafted out of college and came off the bench to begin the season. She was not an All-Star this year. But over the course of the weekend, she got a taste of the star treatment that could be in her future.</p><p>She interviewed with ESPN at WNBA Live and met with AAU players in town for the Nike Classic. The weekend’s most memorable introduction came during a private gathering, when Taylor and her teammates <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/07/24/barack-obama-gives-wnba-all-stars-wisdom-and-a-little-presidential-aura" >met former President Barack Obama</a>.</p><p>“I told my parents his presence, when he walked in the room alone, was very breathtaking,” Taylor said. “I feel like I had to straighten up and act right.</p><p>“He’s a big part of history.”</p><p>Taylor’s rise could hardly have come at a more important time for the Sky.</p><p>They are in their third consecutive losing season, and for the first time in the organization’s 21-year history, they went without an All-Star.</p><p>They need to find their next generation of stars.</p><p>Before tearing her ACL, forward Rickea Jackson appeared ready to become one of them. Third-year center Kamilla Cardoso has also taken a significant step forward and came closest to earning an All-Star nod.</p><p>Taylor’s emergence gives the Sky another possibility.</p><p>She is already tied with veteran Skylar Diggins for the team lead at 14.2 points per game.</p><p>But maybe the most important thing about Taylor is that she always wants more.</p><p>When she was coming off the bench, she was unafraid to say she wanted more minutes. Now she is just as comfortable acknowledging that she wants more opportunities to close out games.</p><p>“I love doing that,” Taylor said. “It’s who I am. I enjoy taking those type of shots. I like the ball in my hands late in the game, being able to create, not just for myself but for my teammates.</p><p>“Growing up, I’ve always been that kind of player. You stay in the driveway and you’re counting down, 3, 2, 1, and you throw up a crazy shot.”</p><p>As her profile has risen, Taylor said former coaches from childhood have reached out. None have been surprised to see her thriving at this level.</p><p>Since moving into the starting lineup midway through the season, Taylor is averaging 17.9 points while shooting 48.1% from the field and 39.4% from three-point range. She’s already made multiple last-second three-pointers to give the Sky a chance to win.</p><p>It’s all still a relatively small sample. But coach Tyler Marsh said this week he wants to give Taylor more chances to become the team’s “closer.” And if she continues playing this way, her All-Star case will write itself.</p><p>Taylor is not afraid to say it.</p><p>She wants to be an All-Star next year.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true"
