entries.title: Lake View man sues feds for raiding his home, arresting construction worker during Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>A Lake View man sued the federal government Tuesday alleging that immigration agents entered his home without a warrant and arrested a construction worker he’d hired at the height of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign last fall.</p><p>Leo Feler was traveling for work on the morning of Oct. 24 when he turned on his Ring camera and saw masked federal agents descending on his home in the 3300 block of North Lakewood Avenue, according to the federal lawsuit. They were chasing a group of workers Feler had hired to repair windows. </p><p>Using the camera’s microphone, Feler told the agents they were trespassing and demanded they get off his property, according to the lawsuit. A tenant, who was home at the time, also demanded a warrant but was ignored.</p><p>One worker was arrested by federal agents, and dozens of Feler’s neighbors were tear-gassed while protesting. Feler returned home to find several “puddles of blood” and tens of thousands of dollars in damage to his property, according to the lawsuit. </p> <p>He’s seeking damages from the federal government and all individual agents involved.</p><p>“There was no reason for this raid to be happening on my property,” Feler told reporters at a news conference Tuesday outside his home. “There was nothing illegal that had been happening on my property. It was just workers doing construction.”</p><p>U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents had already <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/immigration-agents-arrest-lake-view-protest-tear-gas" target="_blank" >torn through several other North Side neighborhoods</a> that morning.</p><p>Then they sped the wrong way down Feler’s quiet Lake View block and spotted four workers “peacefully eating lunch” outside his home, according to the lawsuit. Agents poured out of two vans and began chasing the workers, who ran behind Feler’s 6-foot fence and closed the gate. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dKXPordbAnc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Feds make arrests, deploy tear gas in Lake View"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Unable to break the gate’s lock, agents began scaling the fence and chasing the workers through Feler’s property, entering his backyard, balcony and detached garage, the lawsuit says. One of the four workers was followed into the garage and detained.</p><p>When agents brought the worker back to the front, dozens of neighbors had gathered outside protesting the arrest and demanding to see a warrant. As agents continued down the street, they launched at least two canisters of tear gas into the group of neighbors. Witnesses reported hearing no warning before the gas was deployed.</p><p>“At the very end of the raid, when these federal agents were backing up, without anyone blocking them from backing up, you could hear them yelling, ‘Throw the tear gas just for fun,’” Feler said.</p><p>“That gives you a sense of what this raid was all about,” he added. “This was just for fun for them, but it was traumatic for me.”</p><p>After the raid, the government admitted it didn’t have a warrant or any reason to believe that any criminal activity was happening on or near Feler’s property, according to the lawsuit. Feler began working with an immigration attorney to provide support to the worker who’d been detained. He later learned the worker had no criminal history and had been paying taxes. The worker was ordered released from federal custody three weeks after the arrest.</p><p>Feler previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/31/lake-view-federal-cpd-immigration-raid" target="_blank" >attempted to file</a> a report with Chicago police but said he was essentially turned away at the station — twice. One station allowed him to file a report for criminal damage to property but later called to inform him that police would not pursue the case.</p><p>“So here I am now,” Feler said. “And I’m bringing this case out of respect, admiration and duty to my country, to our Constitution, to my neighbors who were tear-gassed as they were trying to defend my home, to my tenants who had to endure the raid … to my family and to myself.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/x0ItYUijCgk?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago Homeowner Sues After Warrantless CBP Raid | Press Conference"></iframe> </div> </div></div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/31/lake-view-federal-cpd-immigration-raid" target="_blank" >Lake View man wants the Chicago police to investigate feds who entered his property during raid</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/immigration-agents-arrest-lake-view-protest-tear-gas" target="_blank" >Feds make arrests across North and Near West sides, deploy tear gas on residential street in Lake View</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Patients call on Pritzker to reopen Weiss, West Suburban hospitals
entries.summary: <p>Chicago's Uptown and Austin communities have each been down a safety-net hospital for months. </p><p>In Uptown, it's been nearly a year since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/08/08/weiss-memorial-hospital-emergency-room-in-uptown-closes" target="_blank" >Weiss Memorial Hospital closed its doors</a>. In Austin, it's been four months since West Suburban Medical Center on the eastern edge of Oak Park <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/03/25/west-suburban-medical-center-closing-runs-out-cash-weiss-memorial" target="_blank" >stopped serving patients</a>. </p><p>Meanwhile, the two owners of both hospitals have been locked in a bitter legal battle in Cook County court for months.</p><p>Stuck on the sidelines are patients like Phong Nguyen.</p><p>The 81-year-old Vietnamese refugee and longtime Uptown resident depended on Weiss for years to treat conditions including arthritis and tuberculosis.</p><p>"When Weiss closed last August, I was there fighting to reopen this very important hospital," Nguyen said through a translator during a Tuesday rally at Daley Plaza. "Now, almost a year later, I am still here with my community and neighbors, still fighting for our hospital that we have lost. ... I stand with everyone today to make it clear: This is a public health emergency. People's lives, health and jobs are at stake."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ad0000" saying, “This is a public health emergency. People’s lives, health and jobs are at stake.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nguyen shared his story alongside advocates from the North and West sides who say their already vulnerable communities are facing further harm after losing their safety-net hospitals. They called on Gov. JB Pritkzer to intervene and reopen both hospitals under new management. </p><p>Their rally came hours before an afternoon hearing at the Daley Center in the legal fight between Resilience Healthcare chief executive officer Manoj Prasad and the hospitals' landlord, Rathnakar Reddy Patlola. </p><p>Lawyers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/14/west-suburban-medical-center-settlement-cook-county-court" target="_blank" >continue to argue over a motion</a> pressing Prasad’s legal team to accept a settlement agreement that was finalized in late May. The motion accuses Prasad of delaying the process. The terms of the settlement are sealed. </p><p>"The longer this takes, the harder it's going to be to reopen these hospitals," Scott Kaplan, a lawyer for Patlola, said in court Tuesday. </p><p>Lawyers for Prasad said they need more time to go over the settlement with him. The next hearing is scheduled for Friday afternoon.</p><p>Prasad's lawyers also said Resilience has settled an outstanding bill of $60,000 with ComEd. The utility had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/22/west-suburban-medical-center-unpaid-electric-bills-comed" target="_blank" >threatened to cut off power</a> at West Suburban and Weiss. </p><p>Meanwhile, West Suburban formally laid off 589 employees earlier this month, according to a notice sent to the state. Those employees had been furloughed since late March when the hospital closed. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/26/west-suburban-medical-center-oak-park-prasad-patlola-resilience-healthcare" target="_blank" >West Suburban Medical Center’s closing triggered a legal battle between its owners</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" >‘Where do they go?’ What West Side patients face after their hospital closes.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>During the rally, speakers pleaded with Pritzker to help reopen the hospitals. </p><p>"Today, I call on our state leadership, Gov. Pritzker, to step in and do everything in his power to save our hospitals," Weiss patient Nguyen said. "Gov. Pritzker, where are you? Meet with us. Work with our communities to address this health crisis."</p><p>Pritzker's office, in a written statement, said responsibility to reopen the hospitals falls on its owners.</p><p>"Despite intensive financial and operational support from the State of Illinois throughout Resilience Health's tenure, West Suburban and Weiss Hospitals are ultimately private facilities whose leadership was both unable and unwilling to do everything in their power necessary to keep their facilities in operation — and they never presented the State with any formal request or viable plan to continue operations," Pritzker's office said.</p><p>Advocates also criticized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/27/a-new-illinois-law-keeps-hospital-finances-hidden-from-the-public" target="_blank" >a new state law that requires hospitals</a> to disclose more financial information with state regulators, but not the public.</p><p>"Pritzker just signed a law that they're bragging about, that they say will help have more accountability for these safety-net hospitals toward the state," said Mark Kaplan of North Side Action for Justice. "One of the very baffling things in this law is that there actually is no right for the public, for us, to see what the finances are. ... We don't believe we can leave it up to the good graces of the state. They're the ones that got us in this mess."</p><p>Kaplan and others also condemned the recent decision by the Illinois Health Facilities and Services Review Board to give Resilience more time to improve Weiss before the state permanently revokes its license. </p><p>"How do you not hold [Prasad] accountable of what he did the last five years to give him six more months to finish running Weiss down into the ground?" said the Rev. Robin Hood, founder of Mothers Opposed to Violence Everywhere, at the Daley Plaza rally.</p><p>"Prasad has been a facade all this time," Hood added.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Developers break ground on Chicago’s first all-electric geothermal apartment tower
entries.summary: <p>The developers behind Chicago’s first geothermal and all-electric apartment tower broke ground Tuesday, at a time where the city sorely needs more apartment construction.</p><p>The groundbreaking comes more than three years after Tree Street Group, alongside Magellan Development Group, began planning 410 N. Elizabeth, a two-tower development that will total more than 724 apartments when complete. The project is backed by a $102 million construction loan that the developers secured earlier this month.</p><p>Tuesday’s groundbreaking marked the beginning of the first tower’s construction. The 33-story apartment building will add 383 units to Fulton Market, with 77 of them affordable. Units include 38 studios, 87 one-bedroom, 256 two-bedroom and two three-bedroom apartments. </p><p>Also included at the site is 28,000 square feet of public green space — a rarity in the industrial Fulton Market area — that will include outdoor retail, event space and a dog park.</p><p>“For generations, [this site] served the rail yard, the warehouses and the industries that really built this city,” said Ed Kruschka, principal of Tree Street Group. “And today, we write a new chapter — not with another warehouse, but with a project that really embodies the future of Chicago.”</p><p>Ted Weldon, principal of Tree Street Group, said the developer’s vision was to construct a more efficient building — something city leaders praised during Tuesday’s groundbreaking.</p><p>The building’s geothermal energy system will support more than 80% of the building’s heating, cooling and hot water supply, according to Weldon. The geothermal system, along with other key design features, will slash energy usage by roughly 60% and energy costs by more than 25%.</p><p>The building is projected to reduce emissions by 30%, the equivalent of 390 tons of carbon annually, Weldon said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" which will be the city’s first all-electric, geothermal multifamily high-rise.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Archeo Design Studio</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“We should ask ourselves how a building can use less energy and place less strain on the grid. Consistently, that should be the standard,” said Ald. Walter R. Burnett (27th). “We should ask how design can lower long-term operating costs, and we should ask how innovation can help us deliver better homes in less time. When a building uses energy effectively, residents can face lower utility costs, owners gain more predictable operating [expenses] and rents come down. That is what Chicago needs — point-blank, period. We need more housing, and we need it to be affordable. And we need to build those homes effectively, efficiently and quickly.”</p><p>The construction of 410 N. Elizabeth comes at a time when new apartment stock is sorely needed in Chicago. The average monthly rent for an apartment in Chicago is $2,521, according to July 2 data from RentCafe. That’s up 4.6% compared to the same time last year, when the average rent was $2,410.</p><p>Rents are rising, in part, because of a lack of new construction as demand for apartments increases. RentCafe data also shows 95.3% of apartments across the city are occupied, leaving a small number of units available for those looking to rent. And new construction accounts for only 0.2% of all apartments across Chicago, meaning there’s no new apartments to satiate the growing rental pool.</p><p>“We’re proud of the work we’ve done here, and we’re excited to add a new building to the Chicago skyline at a time when it desperately needs more,” J.R. Berger, president of Magellan Development, said.</p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker signs Illinois school cellphone ban into law to make classrooms 'more conducive to learning'
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker signed legislation Tuesday intended to keep students’ eyes off their phones and on their schoolwork, adding Illinois to the list of states that ban distracting devices in the classroom.</p><p>All local school districts will be required to institute bell-to-bell cellphone bans, though high schools will have the option of limiting access to lunch and passing periods, in order to restrict “the disruption that smartphones create throughout the school day,” Pritzker said at an Elgin press conference.</p><p>“We're making our classrooms more focused, more productive, more conducive to learning,” Pritzker said, pointing to districts across the state that have implemented their own bans and already “seen improvements in academic performance, in student engagement and overall well-being.</p><p>“Bullying declines, grade-point averages improve, AP scores increase,” Pritzker said before signing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/02/18/jb-pritzker-budget-proposal-state-of-state-social-media-tax" target="_blank" ><u>one of his top legislative priorities</u></a> of the year. “Students spend more time connecting with one another instead of scrolling past one another.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure JB Pritzker signs legislation Tuesday requiring school districts to ban cellphones during class time. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>State of Illinois livestream</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The legislation sailed through the Illinois General Assembly during the spring session, a year after stalling out in Springfield — while at least 35 other states have restricted cellphone access in schools.</p><p>Illinois’ law <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/02/what-you-need-to-know-about-illinois-new-cellphone-ban-in-schools" target="_blank" ><u>makes exceptions</u></a> for students with devices deemed necessary by medical professionals; students on 504 or individualized education plans (IEPs); English language learners who need them for translation; and students who are caregivers for a family member.</p><p>Teachers can also allow devices to be used in lessons and in case of emergencies. Districts are required to account for providing access in their “emergency and crisis response plans, protocols, or procedures,” the law states.</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Education will release a template cellphone policy later this summer to spur community discussions in local school districts.</p><p>Schools will be required to implement their own cellphone bans by the start of the 2027-28 academic year, extending beyond cellphones to tablets, personal laptops, gaming devices, smartwatches, smart glasses and other electronics.</p><p>School districts that previously instituted bans will have to be fully aligned with state standards by the 2031-32 school year.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/02/21/chicago-students-share-mixed-feelings-on-pritzker-proposal-to-restrict-classroom-use-of-cellphones" >Chicago students share mixed feelings on Pritzker proposal to restrict classroom use of cellphones</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Nearly three-quarters of high school teachers who responded to a 2024 Pew Research poll called phone distraction a major problem.</p><p>Preliminary academic research on cellphone bans has been mixed. A study earlier this year by the <a class="Link" href="https://tom-dee.github.io/files/w35132.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>National Bureau of Economic Research</u></a> found that a reduction in phone usage made a minimal impact on test scores and attendance.</p><p>But Elgin School District U-46 Supt. Suzanne Johnson said the impact was evident when her district cracked down on cellphones last year.</p><p>“While at first our students were probably hesitant and maybe not so pleased, they quickly adjusted to the new learning environment,” Johnson said at Pritzker’s press conference. “Without the distraction of cellphones, students were more engaged, built stronger connections with one another, and once again, laughter and chatter filled our hallways, our cafeteria, and our classrooms. Teachers told us that they finally felt they had their students back.”</p><p>The governor agreed the anecdotal evidence is prevalent.</p><p>“Parents have been concerned and have seen cyberbullying and, of course, the mental health impact that social media and phone usage are having on our kids,” Pritzker said. “Students share that concern.”</p><p>“We want to make sure that every hour of school time can have the greatest possible positive impact. We're allowing every child to fully learn, participate, ask questions and build the skills and interpersonal relationships that they need to thrive.”</p>
